rows.verified: Employers are expected to complete a first-aid needs assessment.
The needs assessment determines whether an appointed person or suitably trained first-aiders are required.
Employers should provide adequate first-aid facilities and a suitably stocked first-aid box.
Workers should receive information about the workplace first-aid arrangements.
Where a first-aider is not required, an appointed person can take charge of equipment, facilities and emergency-service calls.
First-aid box contents should reflect the first-aid needs assessment rather than a universal fixed list.
Employers remain responsible for first-aid needs of travelling, remote and mobile employees.
First-aider numbers and training level should be based on the workplace first-aid needs assessment.
First-aid provision depends on hazards, workforce size, work patterns, remoteness and foreseeable incidents at the actual workplace.
First-aid evidence is workplace- and workforce-specific and is not an exact parcel-level emergency-readiness probability.
Employers must manage health and safety risks before people work alone, including contracted and self-employed workers.
Lone workers work without close or direct supervision and may include drivers, health workers, engineers, cleaners and home workers.
Lone workers may face greater consequences when something goes wrong because immediate support is not available.
Employers must train, supervise and monitor lone workers.
Employers should keep in touch with lone workers and have arrangements to respond to incidents.
Risk assessment should consider violence, stress, medical suitability and isolated or rural workplaces.
Some high-risk activities require another person, including certain confined-space, live electrical, diving, explosives and fumigation work.
Supervision levels should be based on risk, with higher-risk work receiving more supervision.
The monitoring, communication and emergency arrangements must match the worker, task, location, schedule and foreseeable loss-of-contact scenario.
Lone-working evidence is person-, task- and organisation-specific and is not an exact parcel-level safety probability.
